sections.body:
Our office is in Gilbert, and we have been roofing in the Valley since 1993. Most of our jobs are in the East Valley, where we can reach a home quickly and come back easily for follow-up work. We also take jobs across the wider Phoenix area.

We have detailed pages for our three busiest cities. Each one covers the age of local homes, common roof types, monsoon and heat concerns, and how permits and HOA approval usually work there.
bullets: Mesa: see roofing in Mesa, AZ
Chandler: see roofing in Chandler, AZ
Gilbert: see roofing in Gilbert, AZ
Also served: Queen Creek, San Tan Valley, Tempe, Phoenix, Scottsdale, Apache Junction, Ahwatukee, Glendale and Peoria

sections.body:
Mesa is the oldest and largest of the three. It was founded in 1878, and its population grew from 63,049 in 1970 to 288,091 in 1990. That means many Mesa neighborhoods have roofs that are 30 years old or more, plus a large set of 55+ communities with older shingle and low-slope roofs. East Mesa also has brand-new master-planned communities such as Eastmark.

Chandler grew fastest in the 1980s and 1990s, from 29,673 residents in 1980 to 176,581 in 2000. Much of the city is concrete tile on homes from that era, now reaching the age when the underlayment beneath the tile needs attention.

Gilbert is the youngest. It had 5,717 residents in 1980 and 267,918 in 2020. Most homes are tile-roofed production homes from the mid-1980s on, and nearly every neighborhood has an HOA.

sections.h2: Common roof types in the East Valley
sections.body: Concrete tile on a sloped roof is the most common roof we see on East Valley homes, especially on houses built from the late 1980s on. Older homes and many 55+ communities often have asphalt shingles, and a lot of homes in every era have a flat or low-slope section over a patio, addition or Territorial-style roofline.
bullets: Tile roofs (concrete and clay): the tile lasts a long time, but the underlayment beneath it wears out and eventually needs a lift and relay
Asphalt shingles: common on older homes and many retirement communities; heat and UV shorten their life
Spray foam roofs: common on flat sections and Territorial-style homes; the protective coating needs periodic recoating
Flat roofs and elastomeric coatings: patio covers, additions and commercial buildings

sections.body:
Arizona's monsoon season officially runs June 15–September 30. Storms bring sudden wind, dust and short bursts of heavy rain, and that is when we see the most broken tiles, lifted shingles and leaks at flashing. Average July highs in Mesa, Chandler and Gilbert are all around 106°F, and that heat, along with strong UV, wears down shingles, foam coatings and exposed underlayment year-round.

The best time to find problems is before the season starts. A spring roof inspection catches slipped tiles, cracked flashing and worn coatings while they are still small repairs. After a big storm, check your ceilings and yard for signs of damage and see our damaged roof page.

Re-roofing in the Valley is regulated by each city's building department, and the rules depend on the city and the scope of the job. Some communities with East Valley mailing addresses, such as Sun Lakes and several Mesa county islands, are unincorporated, so permitting goes through Maricopa County instead. We confirm what is required for your address before work starts.

If your home is in an HOA, you usually need architectural approval before changing roof color, tile profile or material. We can give you the product details your HOA asks for. Some condo and townhome associations handle roof replacement themselves, so check your CC&Rs first.

We handle residential and commercial roofing on tile, shingle, foam, flat and coated roofs. Financing is available, and you can ask about it during your estimate. For cost questions, start with our roofing cost guide; every roof is different, so a real number comes from an inspection.

sections.body:
Mesa was founded in 1878 and incorporated in 1883. It counted 504,258 residents in the 2020 census, making it the third-largest city in Arizona. Most of that growth came fast: the population went from 63,049 in 1970 to 152,453 in 1980, 288,091 in 1990 and 396,375 in 2000.

That history shapes the roofing work here. A large share of Mesa's neighborhoods went up in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, so many roofs are now 25 to 50 years old. On those homes we see a lot of tile underlayment replacement, shingle re-roofs and worn flat sections. In southeast Mesa, communities such as Eastmark (opened in 2013) and Cadence at Gateway (first phase 2018) are still young, and the work there is mostly storm repairs and small fixes.

sections.h2: Common roof types by era of homes
sections.body: Roof type in Mesa tracks closely with when a neighborhood was built. Here is what we typically find, with examples drawn from public listing records:
bullets: 1950s–1970s homes and early retirement communities: composition shingles and low-slope sections. Listings in Mesa Grande (1969), Sunland Village (built 1974–1984) and Dreamland Villa (opened 1959) show composition roofs.

1970s–1980s master-planned communities: Dobson Ranch, one of Mesa's oldest master-planned communities, was built between 1973 and 1999. Homes of this era usually have shingle or tile pitched roofs, often with a flat patio section.
Late 1980s–1990s subdivisions: concrete tile becomes standard. Listings in Alta Mesa (1988), Red Mountain Ranch (1994), Superstition Springs (1995) and Augusta Ranch (1999) show concrete tile.
Foothill and custom homes: Las Sendas homes from the late 1990s on use concrete tile, while some Territorial-style custom homes in the northeast foothills have flat foam roofs.
2010s to today: concrete tile on production homes in Eastmark, Cadence at Gateway and Mountain Bridge.

sections.h2: What older tile roofs in Mesa need
sections.body:
Concrete tile can outlast the house, but it is not the waterproof layer. The underlayment beneath the tile does that job, and it dries out and cracks with age and heat. On Mesa homes from the 1990s or earlier, the original underlayment is often at or past the end of its life even when the tile looks fine from the street.

The fix is usually a tile underlayment replacement, also called a re-felt or lift and relay: we remove the tile, install new underlayment and flashing, and reset the good tile. It costs less than a full replacement and keeps the look your HOA approved. See our roofing cost guide for how pricing works.

Mesa summers are long and hot. At the East Mesa weather station, the average high is 104.1°F in June, 105.9°F in July and 104.6°F in August, and the record is 121°F. That heat and the strong UV break down shingles, foam coatings and any underlayment exposed at edges and valleys.

Mesa averages about 10.76 inches of rain a year, and July, August and September are the wettest months. That rain mostly arrives in monsoon storms between June 15 and September 30, often with high wind and blowing debris. One storm can crack tiles, lift shingles and push water past tired flashing.

Not every Mesa address is in the city. Leisure World and Dreamland Villa are unincorporated Maricopa County islands surrounded by Mesa, so building permits there go through the county.

Many Mesa neighborhoods also have HOA rules. Las Sendas, for example, has an architectural review process and published CC&Rs, so plan for approval before changing tile color or profile. In some condo associations, such as certain sections of Sunland Village East, roof replacement is included in the HOA fee and the association handles it. Check your CC&Rs before you schedule work.
We work on homes and commercial buildings across Mesa, on tile, shingle, foam, flat and coated roofs. Financing is available; ask about it during your estimate.

sections.body:
Chandler started as a ranch. Alexander J. Chandler, the first veterinary surgeon in the Arizona Territory, settled here in 1891, the town-site office opened in 1912, and the town was incorporated in 1920. For decades it stayed small: Chandler had 29,673 residents in 1980.

Then it boomed. By 2000 the population was 176,581, nearly six times the 1980 count, and the 2020 census counted 275,987. Intel, the city's largest employer with 12,000 workers, anchors a tech economy that drove much of that growth.

For roofing, that means a large share of Chandler's homes date from the late 1980s through the mid-2000s. Most have concrete tile, and many are now 20 to 35 years old. The tile often still looks good, but the underlayment beneath it is wearing out, so tile underlayment replacement is one of the most common jobs we do here.

sections.h2: Common roof types by era of homes
sections.body: Here is what we usually find in Chandler, with examples drawn from public listing records:
bullets: Late 1980s homes in north and west Chandler: a mix of shingle and tile. A 1987 home in Twelve Oaks near the Intel campus has composition shingles, while a 1987 home in Andersen Springs has tile.
1990s master-planned communities: concrete tile is standard. Ocotillo, with homes mostly from the 1990s and 2000s, and The Provinces, Clemente Ranch and Fox Crossing all show tile on listings.
2000s south Chandler: concrete tile on communities such as Fulton Ranch (begun 2005), Sun Groves, Cooper Commons and Valencia.
Custom and estate homes: tile with flat sections. Listings in Whitewing at Krueger show a foam roof on one home and tile with hot-mopped flat sections on another.
55+ communities: Springfield (built 1996–2000) and Solera (2001–2005) have tile. Older Sun Lakes homes include foam and built-up flat roofs.

sections.h2: Why tile underlayment matters in Chandler
sections.body:
On a tile roof, the underlayment is the real waterproof layer. The tile shields it from sun and sheds most of the water, but heat slowly dries the underlayment out until it cracks and lets water through, usually at valleys, around penetrations and along the lower edges of the roof.

Since so many Chandler homes were built in the same 15–20 years, whole neighborhoods tend to reach this point together. A lift and relay replaces the underlayment and flashing and reuses the sound tile. It usually costs less than a full re-roof and keeps your home's original look. Our roofing cost guide explains how pricing works.

Chandler's average July high is 106°F, and the record is 119°F. The city averages about 9.20 inches of rain a year. Much of that falls during monsoon season, June 15–September 30, when storms bring strong wind, dust and short, heavy downpours.

Heat and UV do slow damage all year: shingles lose granules, foam coatings wear thin and exposed underlayment breaks down. Monsoon storms do fast damage: cracked and slipped tile, lifted shingles, debris in valleys and water forced past old flashing.

Do I need HOA approval for a new roof in Gilbert?

Usually, if you are changing color, tile profile or material. Gilbert has roughly 200 registered HOAs and neighborhoods, and most have an architectural review process. We can supply product details for your application.
Does my HOA handle my roof?

It depends on your community and home type. In some associations, such as townhomes and patio homes in The Islands, the HOA covers roofs. Single-family owners are usually responsible for their own. Check your CC&Rs.
When is monsoon season in Gilbert?
Monsoon season officially runs June 15–September 30. Storms bring wind, dust and heavy rain and cause most of the storm damage we repair.
What should I do if a storm damages my roof?

Take photos from the ground, check your ceilings, and stay off the roof. Then call us at 602-548-3770 during office hours. If we don't answer, leave a message and we'll return your call within 24 hours.
Do you work on homes in the Heritage District?
Yes. Homes near downtown Gilbert range from older houses to new infill, so we see shingle, tile and flat roofs there. We work on all of them.
How much does a roof cost in Gilbert?
Every roof is different, so the price comes from an inspection. Our roofing cost guide explains what affects price, including size, material, pitch and decking condition.
Do you offer financing?
Yes, financing is available. Ask about it when we give you your estimate.
